name: Familial Hyperphosphatemic Tumoral Calcinosis / Hyperphosphatemic Hyperostosis Syndrome

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Diagnostic Criteria for Familial Hyperphosphatemic Tumoral Calcinosis

criteria.description: Persistent elevated serum phosphate levels above normal reference range
Presence of periarticular calcified masses typically around large joints
Positive family history consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance
Normal serum calcium levels despite hyperphosphatemia
Radiographic evidence of hyperostosis and cortical thickening of long bones

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of hyperphosphatemia, tumoral calcinosis lesions, and radiologic hyperostosis
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing for mutations in GALNT3, FGF23, or KL genes can confirm diagnosis

pathognomonic.notes: Firm, painless calcified masses near large joints such as hips, elbows, and shoulders
Elevated serum phosphate levels without corresponding hypercalcemia
Cortical thickening and periosteal reaction visible on X-rays
searchTerms: excessive bone growth on long bones

common.symptomName: Joint stiffness and limited range of motion
common.notes: Due to calcified masses restricting joint mobility
Calcified nodules palpable under the skin near affected joints

common.symptomName: Bone pain localized to affected areas
common.notes: Intermittent or chronic pain associated with hyperostosis
Helps differentiate from other metabolic bone diseases

occasional.notes: Secondary to joint involvement and chronic inflammation
Elevated inflammatory markers in some patients
Rarely, masses may ulcerate causing secondary infection
searchTerms: open wounds on hardened skin areas

occasional.notes: Delayed growth due to chronic disease burden

rare.notes: Due to bone fragility in advanced disease
Rare compensatory response to phosphate retention

laboratory: Elevated serum phosphate levels persistently above normal
Normal or mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase
imaging: Radiographic evidence of cortical hyperostosis and periosteal reaction
CT or MRI may delineate extent of soft tissue calcifications
other: Family history consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance
Histopathology of calcified masses showing calcium phosphate deposits

distinguishingFeatures: Associated with chronic renal failure or hyperparathyroidism
Localized calcium deposits in skin without systemic phosphate abnormalities
Often associated with connective tissue diseases
Localized thickening of frontal bone only

redFlags: Rapid enlargement of periarticular calcified masses causing neurovascular compromise
Ulceration or infection of calcified masses
Severe joint immobility leading to functional impairment
references: Topaz O, et al. Mutations in GALNT3, encoding a protein involved in O-linked glycosylation, cause familial tumoral calcinosis. Nat Genet. 2004.
Ichikawa S, et al. Hyperphosphatemic familial tumoral calcinosis: clinical and genetic features. J Bone Miner Metab. 2011.
Orphanet: Familial hyperphosphatemic tumoral calcinosis / Hyperphosphatemic hyperostosis syndrome. ORPHA:306661.
